intro: Southeast Asia is home to many fighting arts with their own names: Muay Thai in Thailand, lethwei in Myanmar, pencak silat in Indonesia, silat in Malaysia, arnis in the Philippines and Vovinam in Vietnam. Each grew in its own place, under its own kings, colonial rulers and new governments. In this unit you will study the objects, stadiums, laws and federations that shaped them.

These arts also traveled. Filipino workers carried eskrima to California. Indo families carried silat to the Netherlands. Thai trainers opened gyms around the world, and refugees carried Vovinam abroad. Some arts came to Chicago. By the end of the unit, you can name each art's place, explain its key objects and laws, and compare a village festival with a city gym.
bigQuestion: What happens to a martial art's objects and rules when it moves from its home to a nation's stadiums and then to gyms around the world?

title: Southeast Asia and Travel

chapters.title: Muay Thai Objects
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the objects of a Thai boxing gym, like the mongkon and the pra jiad, carry history from old Siam into a world sport?

story.title: A Head Hoop on a Ring Plan
story.kicker: On a desk in a Bangkok gym, two small objects sit on top of a drawing of a boxing ring.
paragraphs: A drawing of a boxing ring lies on a desk in a Bangkok gym. It shows four corners, four ropes and a square canvas floor. On top of the drawing sits a stiff loop of rope wrapped in cloth. Beside it lies a thin band of knotted cloth.

The loop is a mongkon, a head hoop. A trainer places it on a fighter's head before a bout. The band is a pra jiad, an armband. Many fighters tie it around the upper arm and wear it during the fight. Neither object is part of the written scoring rules.

The ring plan is modern. Square rings with ropes came to Bangkok in the twentieth century, along with gloves, rounds and weight classes. The hoop and the armband come from older customs. Many Thai gyms treat both as gifts that link a fighter to a teacher, a family and a camp.

In the gym, these objects are not costumes. Trainers keep them on shelves or altars and hand them over with care. Their story shows how one sport kept older marks while it adopted new rules from Western boxing.
story.think: Why might a gym keep an old object even after the rules of the sport have changed?

lessons.title: Fighting Arts in Old Siam
lessons.mainIdea: Long before modern rings, the kingdom of Siam had unarmed and armed fighting arts tied to war and festivals.
reading: Thailand was called Siam until 1939. From 1351 to 1767, its main kingdom had its capital at Ayutthaya, a river city north of today's Bangkok. Soldiers of Ayutthaya trained with swords, spears and staffs, and they also trained to fight without weapons.

Thai people today often call the older unarmed styles *muay boran*, which means ancient boxing. The armed art is called *krabi krabong*, named for the sword and the staff. Both were taught in villages, temples and royal circles, and they were often shown at temple fairs.

Records from these centuries are few. Much of Ayutthaya's written history burned when a Burmese army destroyed the city in 1767. Historians piece together the older arts from later chronicles, paintings, poems and the memories of teaching families.

words.d: the name of the Thai kingdom until 1939
a Thai name for older styles of boxing; it means ancient boxing
a Thai armed art named for the sword and the staff

lessons.title: The Story of Nai Khanom Tom
lessons.mainIdea: Nai Khanom Tom is a famous Thai story about a captured boxer; it is honored as legend and set beside what records show.
reading: After Ayutthaya fell in 1767, many Siamese people were taken to Burma as captives. A well-known story says one of them, *Nai Khanom Tom*, fought Burmese boxers before the Burmese king. In the story he wins match after match and earns his freedom.

The story comes from later retellings, not from a record written at the time of the matches. Historians treat it as a *legend*, a story handed down that may hold some truth but cannot be checked. The details change from one telling to another.

The legend still matters as history of another kind. It shows how Thai people in the twentieth century linked boxing to national pride and survival. Thailand honors Nai Khanom Tom with a yearly boxers' day, and statues of him stand in Ayutthaya province.

words.d: a story handed down over time that cannot be fully checked
a Siamese captive who, in a famous story, won his freedom by boxing in Burma

choices: as a legend that cannot be fully checked

check.why: A legend may hold truth, but it cannot be checked like a record.

check.q: What does the legend show about the twentieth century?

lessons.title: From Bound Cords to Gloves
lessons.mainIdea: In the early twentieth century, Bangkok boxing moved from cord-wrapped hands to gloves, rounds and a roped ring.
reading: In older bouts, fighters wrapped their hands and forearms in long strips of cord or hemp. The Thai name for this wrapping is *kard chuek*. Matches were held in open spaces, such as a temple yard or a cleared field, and a match often ran without set rounds.

In the 1920s and 1930s, Bangkok promoters and officials brought in rules modeled on international boxing. Fighters began to wear padded *gloves*. Bouts were split into timed rounds, and a square ring with ropes replaced the open ground.

Reports of serious injuries in cord bouts pushed these changes forward. Weight classes, taken from Western boxing, later let fighters of similar size meet. The name Muay Thai, meaning Thai boxing, came into wide use as the sport took this new shape.

words.d: cord or hemp wrapped around the hands in older Thai boxing
padded coverings for the hands, brought into Thai boxing in the early 1900s
a timed part of a bout with a rest after it

lessons.title: Two Famous Stadiums
lessons.mainIdea: Rajadamnern Stadium, opened in 1945, and Lumpinee Stadium, opened in 1956, became the centers of Thai professional boxing.
reading: Building on *Rajadamnern Stadium* began in Bangkok in 1941 on a plan from the Thai government. The Second World War slowed the work. The stadium held its first fights in December 1945, and it became the first permanent home for the sport.

*Lumpinee Stadium* opened in 1956 and was run by the Royal Thai Army. For decades, a title belt from Rajadamnern or Lumpinee counted as the top honor for a Thai fighter. Many fighters, trainers and fans still judge a career by these titles.

In 2014 Lumpinee moved to a new building in northern Bangkok. Both stadiums kept their own rules, their own judges and their own rankings. A stadium in this system works like a league: it sets fight nights and names champions.

lessons.title: A Written Bout
lessons.mainIdea: Modern Thai professional bouts follow written rules for rounds, rest and scoring, set by stadiums and later by law.
reading: A professional Muay Thai bout in Thailand usually lasts five rounds. Each round runs three minutes, with a two-minute rest between rounds. Three judges sit beside the ring and score each round, and a referee works inside the ropes.

Stadium rules also name what is allowed and what is a *foul*, a broken rule. Fighters must weigh in before the bout to prove they fit their weight class. Doctors check fighters, and officials record each result.

Fans at the stadiums have long bet on bouts, and the betting shaped how fights were watched. Many Thai fans say early rounds are often slower, and later rounds decide the score. Scoring customs like this are part of the stadium's own culture, and they differ from Olympic-style amateur rules.

words.d: an act that breaks the written rules of a bout
the official weighing of a fighter before a bout
an official who scores each round from beside the ring

lessons.title: The Boxing Act of 1999
lessons.mainIdea: Thailand's Boxing Act of 1999 put professional boxing, including Muay Thai, under national law and a national board.
reading: For most of the twentieth century, each stadium and promoter set its own rules. In 1999 Thailand passed the *Boxing Act*, known in Thailand as the Boxing Act B.E. 2542. B.E. stands for the Buddhist Era, the calendar used for official dates in Thailand.

The law set up a national boxing board under the Sports Authority of Thailand. It required boxers, trainers, gyms, promoters and officials to *register*, or sign up with the government. It also set rules for fighter safety and for young boxers.

The act turned the ring into a licensed public institution. A gym now needed papers, not only a trainer and a floor. Thai lawmakers have since debated changes to the rules for child boxers, a topic that remains part of public argument in Thailand.

lessons.title: The Mongkon
lessons.mainIdea: The mongkon is a head hoop given by a teacher; many gyms treat it as a sign of the camp, not a costume.
reading: The *mongkon* is a stiff loop worn on the head. It is usually made of rope or cord wound tightly and wrapped in cloth, with a tail at the back. In many Thai gyms, the trainer places it on the fighter's head before the bout.

The fighter wears the mongkon while walking to the ring and during the opening ceremony. The trainer then removes it before the first round. Many trainers teach that a fighter should not touch it with the feet or leave it on the floor.

The mongkon links a fighter to a *camp*, the Thai gym where fighters live and train. A camp may keep its mongkon on a shelf or altar between fights. Some gyms outside Thailand now award colored hoops as ranks, a newer custom that Thai stadium camps did not use.

words.d: a head hoop placed on a Thai boxer by the trainer before a bout
a Thai boxing gym where fighters often live and train together

lessons.title: The Pra Jiad
lessons.mainIdea: The pra jiad is an armband many Thai fighters wear during a bout, often described as a gift from family or teacher.
reading: The *pra jiad* is a band of cloth tied around the upper arm. Unlike the mongkon, many fighters keep it on for the whole bout. Some fighters wear one band, and some wear one on each arm.

Thai families and trainers often tell how, in earlier times, a mother tore a strip from her own clothing and tied it on her son's arm before he left to fight. Some bands hold small written prayers or objects inside. Like the mongkon, the pra jiad is described by many fighters as a gift and a reminder of home.

In some gyms outside Thailand, colored armbands mark grades, similar to belts in judo or karate. This is a newer use that grew as Muay Thai spread to other countries. The same object can mean a family gift in one room and a rank in another.

words.d: a cloth armband worn by many Thai boxers during a bout
a level or rank in a system of training

lessons.title: Wai Kru and the Ring Music
lessons.mainIdea: Before a bout, many Thai boxers perform the wai kru ram muay, a ceremony honoring teachers, to live music.
reading: Before a traditional bout, many fighters perform the *wai kru ram muay*. Wai kru means to pay respect to the teacher, and ram muay means boxing dance. Fighters describe it as a way to thank their teachers, their camp and their family.

Each camp may have its own version, so fans can sometimes tell a fighter's gym from the ceremony. The fighter circles the ring and bows in each direction. The mongkon is still on the fighter's head during the ceremony.

Live musicians play during the ceremony and the bout. The group usually includes a *pi java*, a reed pipe, along with two-headed drums and small hand cymbals called ching. The music speeds up as the rounds go on.

words.d: the ceremony before a Thai bout that honors teachers; wai kru means paying respect to the teacher
a reed pipe played in the ring music of Thai boxing
small hand cymbals that keep time in Thai ring music

lessons.title: Neighbors With Their Own Names
lessons.mainIdea: Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos have their own ring arts; each country names and governs its art separately.
reading: Thailand's neighbors have ring arts of their own. In Myanmar, the art is called *lethwei*. It is known for bouts fought with wrapped hands instead of gloves, and for matches at village festivals and pagoda fairs.

In Cambodia, the ring sport is called pradal serey, which means free fighting. Cambodia also has an older art called Kun Lbokator. In 2022 UNESCO added Kun Lbokator to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage, a list of living traditions that countries work to protect.

Neighbors sometimes argue about which country gave a shared practice its start. These arguments show how strongly arts are tied to *national identity*, the sense of what belongs to a nation. Historians compare records from each country rather than choosing a side.

words.d: the ring art of Myanmar, often fought with wrapped hands
an older Cambodian martial art added to UNESCO's heritage list in 2022
a people's sense of what belongs to their nation

lessons.title: From Camp to World Federation
lessons.mainIdea: An international federation for amateur Muaythai grew up and won full recognition from the IOC in 2021.
reading: From the 1970s on, Thai fighters and trainers taught in Japan, Europe, Australia and the United States. Gyms abroad used Thai words and Thai objects, and many sent students to train in Thai camps. Amateur competitions grew beside the professional stadiums.

The *International Federation of Muaythai Associations*, or IFMA, organizes amateur Muaythai around the world. Amateur rules use shorter bouts and require protective gear such as head guards. IFMA writes the sport's name as one word, Muaythai.

The International Olympic Committee gave IFMA provisional recognition in 2016 and full *recognition* in 2021. Recognition means the IOC accepts the federation as the world body for the sport. It does not by itself place the sport in the Olympic Games.

words.d: the world body for amateur Muaythai, known as IFMA
official acceptance of a federation by the International Olympic Committee
competing without being paid, under different rules from professionals

chapters.title: Silat, Arnis, a Chicago Gym
chapters.bigQuestion: How do silat and arnis live both in village ceremonies and in school gyms and city classes far from where they began?

story.title: A Stick on the Closet Shelf
story.kicker: A padded rattan stick sits on a school PE shelf, far from the islands where its art began.
paragraphs: A physical education closet holds balls, cones and jump ropes. On the top shelf lies a bundle of rattan sticks wrapped in foam padding. A label on the bundle reads 'Arnis sticks, set of twenty.' A school ordered them for its PE classes.

Rattan is a climbing palm that grows in the forests of Southeast Asia. In the Philippines, rattan sticks are the best-known object of arnis, also called eskrima or kali. The foam padding is modern. It was added so the stick could be used under sport rules.

In the Philippines, a 2009 law made arnis the national martial art and sport and tied it to school PE. Filipino families also carried the art abroad, to California, Hawaii, Chicago and beyond. A padded stick in a school closet and a teacher's stick at a family gathering come from the same history.

Nearby in Southeast Asia, the silat arts of Indonesia and Malaysia made a similar journey. They moved from village ceremonies to national federations and then to gyms abroad. Both paths are real, and each room keeps its own rules.
story.think: Can an art keep its meaning when it moves from a village ceremony to a school gym? What might change?

lessons.title: One Word, Many Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Silat is a family of fighting arts from the Malay world, taught in hundreds of separate schools.
reading: *Silat* is the name for a large family of fighting arts from the Malay world. That region includes today's Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, along with southern Thailand and the southern Philippines. In Indonesia, the art is usually called *pencak silat*.

There is no single silat. Each school, called a perguruan in Indonesia, has its own teacher line, its own name and its own customs. In West Sumatra, the Minangkabau people call their art silek, and it grew beside village life and the prayer house.

Many silat schools teach with music, and some performances appear at weddings and village feasts. In Malaysia, a silat display often welcomes guests at Malay weddings. These uses sit beside training for self-defense and sport.

words.d: a family of fighting arts from the Malay world
the Indonesian name for silat arts
an Indonesian word for a silat school

look.title: Two Rooms, One Word
look.text: Room 1: in a West Sumatran village, drummers play while two performers move in a circle at a wedding. Room 2: in a Jakarta sports hall, two athletes in padded vests compete while judges score from tables.
look.prompt: What does each room show about silat? Why do both use the same word?

check.q: Which region is the home of silat?
choices: the Malay world of Southeast Asia
check.why: Silat comes from Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore and nearby areas.

check.q: What is a perguruan?
check.why: Perguruan means a silat school in Indonesia.

check.q: What do the Minangkabau of West Sumatra call their art?
check.why: The Minangkabau name is silek.

lessons.title: Silat in a New Nation
lessons.mainIdea: After Indonesia declared independence, IPSI was founded in 1948 to join many silat schools under one national body.
reading: Indonesia declared independence from Dutch colonial rule in 1945. The Netherlands recognized that independence in 1949 after four years of war and talks. The new nation had hundreds of islands and many languages, and its leaders looked for shared symbols.

In 1948 teachers founded *IPSI*, the Indonesian Pencak Silat Association, in the city of Surakarta on Java. IPSI set out to bring many perguruan under one national *federation*. A federation is a group of member schools or clubs that agree to shared rules.

Joining a federation did not erase the old schools. Most kept their own names and teachers. IPSI added a second layer, with national events, shared rules for competition and a voice for silat in government.

words.d: the Indonesian Pencak Silat Association, founded in 1948
a group of member schools or clubs that agree to shared rules
control of a land by a foreign power

lessons.title: From SEA Games to UNESCO
lessons.mainIdea: Pencak silat became an international sport through PERSILAT and regional games, and UNESCO listed silat traditions in 2019.
reading: In 1980 federations from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei founded *PERSILAT*, an international pencak silat body, in Jakarta. Pencak silat entered the Southeast Asian Games in 1987. It joined the Asian Games in 2018, when Indonesia hosted them.
Competition has two kinds of events. In *tanding*, two athletes compete for points. In *seni*, the artistic events, athletes perform set sequences alone, in pairs or in teams, and judges score them.

In December 2019 UNESCO listed two entries on the same day. One was the Traditions of Pencak Silat from Indonesia. The other was Silat from Malaysia. The two listings show that one family of arts can be claimed with pride by more than one nation.

words.d: the international pencak silat federation founded in Jakarta in 1980
the pencak silat event where two athletes compete for points
the pencak silat events judged as artistic performance

lessons.title: Names From Two Languages
lessons.mainIdea: Arnis, eskrima and kali are three names for Filipino stick and blade arts; two of the names come from Spanish.
reading: Spain ruled the Philippines from the 1560s until 1898. During those centuries, Spanish words entered the languages of the islands. Two common names for Filipino stick and blade arts come from Spanish words.

*Arnis* is often traced to arnés, a Spanish word for harness or armor. *Eskrima* comes from esgrima, the Spanish word for fencing. A third name, kali, is widely used in the United States, and teachers disagree about where that word came from.

In the Philippines, arnis is the name most used in schools and in law. Eskrima is common in the Visayas, the central islands, including Cebu. The three names often point to the same family of arts, but each school may prefer one.

words.d: a Filipino stick and blade art; the name used in Philippine law
a name for Filipino stick and blade arts, from the Spanish word for fencing
the central island group of the Philippines, including Cebu

lessons.title: Mactan, 1521
lessons.mainIdea: Pigafetta's record of the 1521 battle at Mactan shows armed island warriors, though it does not describe arnis by name.
reading: In April 1521 the explorer Ferdinand Magellan, sailing for Spain, fought the forces of *Lapulapu*, a leader on the island of Mactan near Cebu. Magellan was killed in the battle. Antonio *Pigafetta*, an Italian who sailed with Magellan, wrote an account of the voyage.

Pigafetta described a large force of island warriors with spears, shields and cutlasses. His account is one of the oldest written records of fighting in the Philippines. It was written by an outsider who survived the loss.

Many Filipino teachers today honor Lapulapu as an early hero of their arts. The account shows that islanders were skilled with weapons in 1521. It does not name arnis or describe a school, so historians keep the link as a tradition rather than a proven line.

words.d: the leader on Mactan whose forces defeated Magellan in 1521
Antonio Pigafetta, the Italian who wrote an account of Magellan's voyage

lessons.title: A National Sport by Law
lessons.mainIdea: In 2009 the Philippines passed Republic Act 9850, naming arnis the national martial art and sport.
reading: In December 2009 the Philippines passed *Republic Act 9850*. The law declared arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines. It named the Department of Education as one agency to carry this out.

The law asked schools to include arnis in physical education. It also asked the Philippine Sports Commission to support arnis competitions. This is how a stick art came to sit in school PE closets across the country.

A law like this is a kind of *national symbol*, a sign that a country uses to describe itself. Other national symbols include flags, anthems and national flowers. Naming a sport in law shows a government choosing which heritage to put forward.

words.d: the 2009 Philippine law that named arnis the national martial art and sport
a sign a country uses to describe itself, like a flag or an anthem

lessons.title: Sport Arnis at the SEA Games
lessons.mainIdea: Arnis became a Southeast Asian Games sport in 2005 using padded sticks, head guards and scored rules.
reading: Arnis first appeared at the Southeast Asian Games in 2005, when the Philippines hosted them. It returned in 2019, again in the Philippines. A host nation may add sports it cares about to the program.

Sport arnis uses *padded sticks* and protective gear such as head guards and body armor. Judges score points under written rules. There are also form events, in which athletes perform set sequences for judges, much like the seni events of pencak silat.
Sport rules make the art safer to compete in and easier to judge. Some teachers say they also narrow what the art includes. The same debate appears in many martial arts that join big sporting events.

words.d: a stick wrapped in foam so it can be used under sport rules
a multi-sport event for the nations of Southeast Asia, held every two years

lessons.title: The Manongs of California and Hawaii
lessons.mainIdea: Filipino workers who came to Hawaii and California in the early 1900s carried eskrima, which later opened to the public.
reading: From 1906, Filipino men came to Hawaii to work on sugar and pineapple plantations. In the 1920s many more came to California to work on farms in places like Stockton and the Salinas Valley. They were later called the *manongs*, from an Ilocano word for older brother.
The manongs faced hard limits. California law barred marriages between Filipinos and white Americans until 1948. Many worked long seasons for low pay and lived in crowded labor camps.

Some manongs practiced eskrima in back yards and union halls, often only with other Filipinos. In the 1960s teachers in Stockton began to open eskrima classes to the public. The art moved from a private family and worker tradition to an American storefront school.

words.d: Filipino men who came to Hawaii and California to work in the early 1900s; the word means older brother
a large farm where many workers grow one crop, such as sugar

lessons.title: Silat in the Netherlands
lessons.mainIdea: After Indonesian independence, Dutch-Indonesian families moved to the Netherlands and brought pencak silat with them.
reading: After Indonesia became independent, about 300,000 people moved from Indonesia to the Netherlands in the 1950s. Many were *Indo* families, people of mixed Dutch and Indonesian descent. They arrived in a cold country that had ruled their birthplace.

Some Indo men had trained in pencak silat in Java. In the Netherlands they opened clubs in cities and towns, often in rented halls. For a time the arts were practiced mostly inside the Indo community.

Later, Dutch students of all backgrounds joined these clubs. The Netherlands became one of the first European centers of pencak silat. This is an example of *diaspora* history, where migrants carry an art and a new country slowly takes part.

words.d: a person of mixed Dutch and Indonesian descent
a person who moves from one country to live in another

lessons.title: Vovinam, From Hanoi Outward
lessons.mainIdea: Vovinam was founded in Hanoi in 1938, and Vietnamese refugees carried it abroad after 1975.
reading: In 1938 Nguyễn Lộc founded *Vovinam* in Hanoi, in what was then French colonial Vietnam. He built it from older Vietnamese fighting arts. He wanted a school art that Vietnamese people could see as their own.

Vovinam grew in southern Vietnam after the country was divided in 1954. When the Vietnam War ended in 1975, many Vietnamese people left as *refugees*, people forced to flee their home country. Teachers among them opened Vovinam clubs in France, the United States and other countries.

Vovinam students wear blue uniforms at many levels, and belt colors mark rank. Today Vovinam has international federations and is a sport at the Southeast Asian Games. It shows a newer art founded under colonial rule becoming part of a diaspora.

words.d: a Vietnamese martial art founded in Hanoi in 1938

lessons.title: A Chicago Room
lessons.mainIdea: Filipino, Thai and other Southeast Asian families in Chicago helped bring these arts into city gyms and classes.
reading: Filipino students came to Chicago in the early 1900s under the pensionado program, which sent them to study at American colleges. The program began in 1903. Filipino workers followed, and Chicago became home to one of the Midwest's largest Filipino communities.

After the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended quotas based on national origin, many more families came from the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. Chicago's Argyle Street area on the North Side became known for Vietnamese and other Southeast Asian shops. New arrivals brought foods, festivals and arts with them.

Today Chicago-area gyms and community programs offer classes in Muay Thai, arnis and silat. A city *gym* runs on schedules, fees and waivers. The same art in a village follows the calendar of festivals and families.

words.d: a Filipino student sent to study in the United States under a program begun in 1903
a U.S. law that ended immigration quotas based on national origin
a room or business for training, with schedules and fees

lessons.title: Both Rooms Are Real
lessons.mainIdea: A village festival and a city gym are different institutions, and each is a real home for the same art.
reading: In West Java, performers show pencak silat to the music of drums and a reed pipe at weddings and community feasts. The drum music for this is called kendang pencak. The performance honors families and guests, and no one keeps a score.

In a city gym in Chicago, Manila or Amsterdam, the same art may be taught for fitness, sport or self-defense. There are sign-up sheets, class times and belt or grade systems. The gym answers to its members and to local laws.

Neither room is fake. Each is an *institution*, a lasting set of people, places and rules. Historians ask which rules each room follows and who decides them, instead of asking which one is the true art.

words.d: a lasting set of people, places and rules, like a school, a club or a festival
the drum music that goes with pencak silat performances in West Java
